cohort.label: 2016–2020 Board
cohort.transition_reason: Swearing-in of the 2016–2020 Board on December 5, 2016 following the November 8, 2016 election. Newly elected commissioners Heidi Carter and James Hill joined returning incumbents Wendy Jacobs, Ellen W. Reckhow, and Brenda A. Howerton, succeeding outgoing commissioners Michael D. Page and Fred Foster Jr. Annual Chair/Vice Chair leadership remained consistent throughout the term: Wendy Jacobs (Chair, Dec 2016–Dec 2020) and James Hill (Vice Chair, Dec 2016–Dec 2020).

conflicts.issue: Full Immediate Funding ($3.8M) for DPS Classified Staff $15/Hour Minimum Wage and FY 2020–2021 Budget Adoption
conflicts.summary: The board split 2-3 on appropriating $3.8 million from reserves to immediately pay all DPS classified staff $15/hour, and subsequently split 3-2 on adopting the final FY 2020–2021 budget ordinance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Fully fund the $15/hour living wage for all DPS classified staff in FY 2020–2021 now using fund balance/COVID reserves, and reject a budget that leaves those workers below $15/hour.
side_a_arguments: DPS bus drivers, custodians, and cafeteria workers—overwhelmingly Black and brown essential workers—were the only remaining county/city public employees below $15/hour.

With $3.5M remaining in the COVID set-aside, $4.6M in economic uncertainty reserves, and expected FEMA/CARES reimbursements for the $3.67M fund balance spend, the county could fund the $3.8M gap immediately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit DPS classified wage increases to the ~$1.9M down payment in the FY21 budget, preserve reserves against pandemic uncertainty, and revisit full funding in January 2021.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners already redirected ~$2M (including $1.25M from Sheriff detention vacancies and vehicles) on top of the manager's $5M DPS increase after DPS's estimate jumped from $1.7M–$1.8M to $3.8M.

County Manager Wendell Davis warned COVID costs already exceeded $7M and DHHS was demanding 10x testing expansion, while the city's sales-tax split change cost the county ~$2.5M and DPS held an $8M fund balance.
conflicts.resolution: Carter's $3.8M amendment failed 2-3, and the amended FY 2020–2021 budget ordinance passed 3-2 with Carter and Jacobs dissenting.

conflicts.issue: Scope of Proposed Comprehensive Plan Policy Evaluating Affordable Housing Impacts of NPOs and Local Historic Districts
conflicts.summary: During consideration of the 2017 Evaluation and Assessment Report, Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow objected to singling out only Neighborhood Protection Overlays (NPOs) and local historic districts for housing affordability impact evaluations and asked to sever or broaden the wording, whereas Commissioner Heidi Carter and Chair Wendy Jacobs argued the targeted policy was an appropriate informational step prompted by City Council's Old West Durham NPO debate.
conflicts.side_a_position: Sever the policy back to the Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) or broaden its wording to evaluate housing affordability impacts across all major land-use changes, not just NPOs and historic districts.
side_a_arguments: Citing Planning Commissioner Tom Miller's comments and National Trust/CityLab research, older smaller buildings in historic districts and NPOs often preserve naturally occurring affordable housing and prevent teardowns.
Targeting only NPOs and historic districts casts an unfair cloud over neighborhood preservation while ignoring rezonings (such as residential-to-commercial) that also affect housing affordability.
The proposed policy had not been discussed at JCCPC and lacked context in the report.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain and approve the policy as drafted so planning staff evaluates the net impact of proposed NPOs and local historic districts on housing affordability and supply.
side_b_arguments: The policy grew directly out of City Council's Old West Durham NPO deliberations, where restrictions on accessory dwelling units and duplexes raised long-term housing supply concerns.
Planning staff already removed the earlier directive requiring staff to recommend denial, leaving only a neutral informational analysis that could also show positive affordability impacts.
Overlay districts impose broad area-wide restrictions distinct from individual parcel rezonings, and Durham City Council had already approved the report 7-0.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by compromise without a split vote: planning staff agreed to consider proposing broadened policy language covering other land-use categories when returning to JCCPC with the evaluation methodology, after which Commissioner Reckhow moved adoption of the 2017 EAR resolution and it passed unanimously 5-0.

conflicts.issue: Community Health Ambassadors Program Funding ($318,244) — Split Vote 4-1
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-1 on allocating $318,244 from the COVID set-aside account for the Recovery and Renewal Task Force's Community Health Ambassadors Program, dividing over program duplication and uncoordinated pandemic spending.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $318,244 allocation from COVID set-aside funds (while pursuing $89,000 in CRF reimbursement) to address urgent racial disparities and workplace/business COVID clusters.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized the proposal emerged directly from minority and immigrant/refugee task force roundtables to reach Latinx and Black businesses and workers lacking resources or trusted health connections.
Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow moved approval to fund the full-year program immediately while instructing staff to offset eligible expenses with CRF funds.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed funding a $318,244 program perceived as duplicating existing county community health workers, masks, and PPE programs without clearer funding and coordination plans.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton questioned why the budget included $60,000 for PPE, $40,000+ for masks, and community health worker positions when the county already employed community health workers and distributed masks.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 4-1 (Jacobs, Carter, Reckhow, Hill Aye; Howerton Nay).

conflicts.issue: Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws, Law Enforcement Role, and Inter-Board Process
conflicts.summary: City and County elected officials clashed sharply over the proposed 24-month Community Safety and Wellness Task Force—dividing over whether it delayed urgent anti-violence action, whether law enforcement should be excluded from voting membership, and whether the rollout respected county partners.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance a 24-month community-driven task force without law enforcement or staff as voting members (using a separate Community Resource Panel instead) and form a three-body drafting team to finalize bylaws.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson argued the task force was community-initiated and designed for ongoing engagement alongside immediate crisis-response audits rather than delaying action for two years, and endorsed Commissioner Reckhow's Community Resource Panel compromise to keep voting seats community-only.
Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Heidi Carter favored county participation, though Jacobs acknowledged the board lacked consensus.
conflicts.side_b_position: Withhold county endorsement until urgent action, genuine community vetting, answers to commissioner questions, and proper respect for law enforcement and county process are addressed.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton—citing the loss of two sons to gun violence—rejected waiting two years for 'more talking and analysis,' objected that five questions she posed remained unanswered and that the city 'threw' a pre-packaged plan at the county, and argued it was not broadly community-vetted.

Vice Chair James Hill questioned why excluding the Police Chief and Sheriff from the panel was a dealbreaker given their professionalism in Durham; Council Member DeDreana Freeman agreed the rollout bypassed county committees and felt disrespectful.

Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow expressed concern after receiving dozens of emails opposing even law enforcement presence on the non-voting resource panel, leaving her unwilling to force a split county vote without adjusting the timeline and engaging PACs.
conflicts.resolution: No committee vote was taken on the task force; Chair Jacobs agreed to circulate an email seeking a commissioner liaison to meet with Mayor Pro Tem Johnson and a school board representative to see if bylaw revisions could resolve the impasse.

conflicts.meeting_title: August 10, 2020 BOCC Regular Session Virtual Meeting
conflicts.issue: Impasse Over Revised Bylaws for the Joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force
conflicts.summary: The board deadlocked without a vote on revised bylaws for the Joint Community Safety and Wellness Task Force, splitting over whether a 24-month body duplicated existing agencies during a homicide crisis and whether excluding law enforcement from voting seats—or even the resource room—undermined collaboration.
conflicts.side_a_position: Form the joint task force with the City and School Board using the revised bylaws and Community Resource Panel to engage residents on non-law-enforcement crisis and violence-prevention solutions.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs argued residents amid the Black Lives Matter movement were clamoring for a community-led voice and suggested shortening the two-year timeline.

Commissioner Heidi Carter warned that county services (public health, CJRC, JCPC, EMS) were central to the work and expressed concern about the county sitting out while City Council and BOE moved ahead.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed creating a new 24-month task force that duplicates existing work, diverts exhausted staff, and faced community backlash over law enforcement involvement.
side_b_arguments: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead opposed the task force as a 'waste of time and a waste of resources' repeating prior reports while three homicides occurred in a single day, urging synergy with CJRC and existing community groups.

Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton refused to wait two years while Black and brown children were dying in the streets, argued the plan lacked broad community vetting and diverted 24/7 pandemic staff, and Vice Chair James Hill concurred.

Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow stated she had sought a 'big tent' compromise with the Community Resource Panel, but was sobered by an avalanche of community emails rejecting even police and sheriff participation in the room, concluding the board should not force a split vote.
conflicts.resolution: Chair Jacobs concluded the board had reached an impasse with no vote taken, deferring an update to the August 11 Joint City-County Committee meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: July 13, 2020 BOCC Regular Session Virtual Meeting
conflicts.issue: Stormwater Utility Fee Non-Residential Agricultural Parcels and Pandemic Outreach
conflicts.summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs sought to delay adoption of the Stormwater Utility Ordinance and Pulled Item 20-0309 until August to address non-digital outreach and agricultural BMP credits for 125 non-residential farm parcels, while the remaining four commissioners voted 4-1 to enact the fee immediately.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay implementation of the non-residential stormwater fee until August to conduct mail/non-virtual farmer outreach and offset the ~$40,000 impact on 125 agricultural parcels with BMP credits.
side_a_arguments: Many farmers do not use computers or Zoom and could not participate in virtual outreach while in-person Farm Bureau and Ruritan meetings were suspended due to COVID-19.
Charging agricultural properties that already implement water-quality BMPs contradicts county farmland preservation programs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Enact the Stormwater Utility Ordinance and accompanying budget item now while developing a future credit program and mailed tax-bill outreach.
side_b_arguments: Exempting one landowner class poses legal equity risks and shifts compliance costs onto residential ratepayers, while the fee is already baked into the adopted FY21 budget.
Staff noted 499 of 624 agricultural parcels already pay only residential rates (capped at $48/year) and the remaining 125 parcels have a median fee of $120/year.
conflicts.resolution: Both Pulled Item 20-0309 and the Stormwater Utility Ordinance passed 4-1, with staff directed to return with a credit structure proposal and continue mailed/direct outreach.

conflicts.meeting_title: July 13, 2020 BOCC Regular Session Virtual Meeting
conflicts.issue: Joint Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws and Law Enforcement Membership
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split over whether to immediately adopt compromise bylaws placing the Sheriff and Police Chief on a non-voting Community Resource Panel or postpone action to resolve demands for voting law enforcement seats and late draft circulation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the revised bylaws immediately, keeping the task force strictly community-led with non-police solutions while engaging the Sheriff and Police Chief on the advisory Resource Panel.
side_a_arguments: Over 100 community residents urged prompt passage aligned with the Beyond Policing report and prior City Council and School Board approvals.
City Council would not approve voting seats for law enforcement on a community task force designed to evaluate alternatives to policing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Postpone approval to the August work session; add the Sheriff and Police Chief as voting members (Hill) or allow adequate time to review late bylaw revisions (Howerton).
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair James Hill stated excluding Durham's African American Sheriff and Police Chief from voting membership was unreasonable and said he would vote No unless they were added.

Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton stated she was unready to vote because revised drafts were emailed too close to the meeting, and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow agreed to pause two weeks rather than split along racial lines over the two African American members' objections.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Chair Jacobs deferred the bylaws to the August work session.

conflicts.issue: Design and City Cost-Sharing of Countywide Property Tax Assistance Program
conflicts.summary: Ahead of the budget vote, commissioners differed over whether the July 13 property tax relief proposal should focus strictly on long-term low-income homeowners alongside a binding City match, or explore broader legally permissible COVID-19 options.
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring forward a model countywide tax assistance program targeting long-term low-income homeowners in time for FY21 tax bills, meeting directly with advocacy groups.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter emphasized helping long-term low-income homeowners stay in their homes and partnering with the City of Durham.
Chair Wendy Jacobs supported consulting community affordable-housing advocates while also addressing COVID-related mortgage/tax hardship.
conflicts.side_b_position: Restrict options to what is legal under the NC Machinery Act, avoid non-needy recipients, and secure a firm 50%+ financial commitment from the City.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow warned the County Attorney advised outright grant programs could expose commissioners to personal liability, and Vice Chair James Hill cautioned against broad relief echoing federal PPP abuses.
Reckhow and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton noted the Mayor's letter lacked an explicit 50% funding commitment even though the City benefited from $2.5M in reallocated sales tax.
conflicts.resolution: Staff was directed to meet with community groups and present legally viable options on July 13, 2020.

conflicts.issue: Opposition Vote on April 13, 2020 Consent Agenda
conflicts.summary: Following item-by-item review of the consent agenda covering COVID-19 state grants, the $3.67 million fund balance appropriation, 300 E. Main St. parking deck contracts, and Elementary School C land acquisition, Vice Chair James Hill registered a dissenting No vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the full consent agenda to fund urgent COVID-19 operations, shelter/PPE procurement, school land acquisition, and parking deck pre-construction.
side_a_arguments: County Manager Wendell Davis, EOC staff, and commissioners emphasized the rainy-day fund balance appropriation was critical for hotel shelter, PPE, sanitization, and FEMA reimbursement documentation, alongside needed school and capital projects.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval of the consent agenda package.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair James Hill stated on the record that he wished to vote No without specifying which consent item he opposed.
conflicts.resolution: Consent agenda passed 4-1.

conflicts.issue: Triangle Trails Initiative Resolution Governance and Accountability
conflicts.summary: Four commissioners supported endorsing the privately funded multi-county Triangle Trails Initiative with added climate and commuting-equity language, while Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton voted No due to unclear organizational accountability.
conflicts.side_a_position: Endorse the Triangle Trails Initiative resolution to establish regional greenway connections for commuting, health, economic development, and climate benefits at no cost to Durham County.
side_a_arguments: Commissioners Ellen W. Reckhow, Wendy Jacobs, and Heidi Carter noted the initiative required no county funds, leveraged private philanthropy through a regional foundation, and supported transportation equity and carbon reduction.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the resolution until leadership, organizational governance, and county responsibility are clearly explained.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton stated the agenda packet lacked sufficient background on the proposed foundation and which entity would be accountable, saying she 'didn't get the essence of it.'
conflicts.resolution: Resolution passed 4-1, with Reckhow tasked with following up on equitable community engagement and governance questions.

conflicts.issue: County Manager Wendell Davis FY 2018-19 Salary Increase and Evaluation Process
conflicts.summary: The board divided 4-1 over setting County Manager Wendell Davis's FY 2018-19 salary at $221,579 (an increase of over $4,000, or roughly 2%), as well as over holding the vote the same night evaluation materials were circulated at 6:00 p.m.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve a 2% salary increase to $221,579 based on the board's mutually adopted evaluation instrument and peer county benchmarks.
side_a_arguments: James Hill noted that peer county managers received 0% to 2% raises (contradicting claims of a 3%–6% floor) and that 48% of county employees received the same 2% 'meets expectations' increase.

Wendy Jacobs cited benchmark data showing $221,579 ranked third highest in base pay behind only Mecklenburg and Wake counties and second highest statewide in total compensation ($324,968.07 including benefits).
Ellen W. Reckhow and Heidi Carter emphasized that the manager co-drafted and agreed to the evaluation instrument, which the entire board—including Howerton—had unanimously adopted the prior year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject limiting the County Manager's increase to ~$4,000 (~2%) and defer the vote to June 25 to allow proper review of same-day materials.
side_b_arguments: Brenda A. Howerton argued the manager exceeded expectations—citing the AAA bond rating, clean audit, 15+ awards, Managing for Results, Pre-K, gun violence reduction, and southern fire consolidation—and deserved 3%–6% rather than less than the board's own 3% budget adjustment.
Howerton protested voting on information distributed at 6:00 p.m. the same evening instead of postponing action until the June 25 meeting.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 4-1, setting the County Manager's FY 2018-19 salary at $221,579.

conflicts.issue: Lack of Codified Community-Benefit Standards in UDO Development Agreements Amendment (TC2000003)
conflicts.summary: While all five commissioners ultimately voted to adopt TC2000003, commissioners debated Planning Commission opposition and whether the ordinance was too vague without explicit criteria defining qualifying community benefits.
conflicts.side_a_position: The draft ordinance language is overly broad and lacks clear standards or community-benefit parameters, fueling Planning Commission opposition and transparency concerns.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow described the text as 'very general, very loose' without guidelines and noted Planning Commission concern that the amendment was fast-tracked for a pending development.

Chair Wendy Jacobs agreed with Planning Commissioner Austin that criteria should not depend solely on who holds office, and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton questioned whether the Planning Commission had voted before staff briefings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff's added environmental and public-hearing safeguards address major transparency concerns, and Durham County should adopt the tool now following City Council's unanimous approval.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter praised staff for protecting environmentally sensitive standards and adding Planning Commission and neighborhood hearing requirements, viewing development agreements as a valuable tool to secure benefits like affordable housing.
Assistant County Attorney Brian Taylor/attorney staff confirmed every agreement still requires board approval and parameters can be refined afterward.
conflicts.resolution: Adopted 5-0 with explicit direction for staff to return at the November work session to develop formal board guidelines on community-benefit criteria.

conflicts.issue: Co-Chair Selection Process for the Joint Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force
conflicts.summary: Commissioners debated whether the task force's co-chairs should be elected by community task force members or remain appointed by elected officials as already approved by City Council and the School Board.
conflicts.side_a_position: Community members on the task force should elect their own chair/co-chairs and vice chair to preserve community autonomy and avoid political interference.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton argued that residents demanded autonomy without elected officials picking leadership, and Vice Chair James Hill concurred that most boards choose their own officers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid delaying appointment advertising or forcing re-approval delays by City Council and the School Board over co-chair wording, and instead advance the recommendation to the joint committee.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners Heidi Carter and Wendy Jacobs noted that City Council and the School Board had already approved the prior bylaws and warned against holding up urgent recruitment while gun violence persisted.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow proposed approving the revised bylaws 5-0 immediately to begin advertising seats while placing the co-chair selection proposal on the October Joint City-County Committee agenda.

conflicts.issue: Governance of My Brother's Keeper (MBK) Durham: Proposed Advisory Board vs. Milestone Advocacy Teams
conflicts.summary: Following a citizen-backed proposal from DeWarren Langley to create an official MBK Durham Advisory Board, MBK Coordinator Edmund Lewis defended his community-driven Milestone Advocacy Teams against adding an unnecessary hierarchy, while commissioners urged collaboration.
conflicts.side_a_position: Maintain MBK Durham's existing Milestone Advocacy Teams structure under staff leadership rather than creating a formal advisory board.
side_a_arguments: MBK Coordinator Edmund Lewis argued an advisory board would duplicate existing work, introduce hierarchy and compassion fatigue, and slow direct action connecting Black young men to CDL, skilled trades, and Durham Tech scholarships.
Commissioner Heidi Carter noted Lewis already had a functioning community structure that community members could join without building a new layer of governance.
conflicts.side_b_position: Engage proponents of the MBK Advisory Board in dialogue to strengthen strategic coordination, accountability, and immediate gap-funding deployment.
side_b_arguments: Citizen commenter Brandon Williams urged an advisory council for annual reporting and strategic alignment.

Chair Wendy Jacobs urged consulting the Milestone Advocacy Teams to deploy immediate crisis gap funding (such as Durham Tech Back to Work) rather than solely long-term endowments, while Commissioners Ellen W. Reckhow and Brenda A. Howerton asked General Manager Deborah Craig-Ray to bring Lewis and Langley together without slowing MBK's momentum.
conflicts.resolution: General Manager Deborah Craig-Ray agreed to convene Edmund Lewis and DeWarren Langley to explore alignment and report back to the board.

conflicts.issue: Using County Libraries and Piecemeal COVID Reserve Spending for HOPE Learning Centers ($405,600)
conflicts.summary: Prior to voting 5-0 for the six-week $405,600 HOPE Learning Centers allocation, commissioners debated why County libraries remained closed, whether ad-hoc reserve spending lacked a comprehensive plan, and how to guarantee seats reached the neediest students.
conflicts.side_a_position: Fund the 338 ready community seats immediately for six weeks while requiring strict outreach and data tracking for DHA, DSS, and Exceptional Children students.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter argued the 338 ready seats would otherwise go to fee-paying families rather than the most vulnerable students if the county delayed.

Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow conditioned her Aye vote on immediate outreach to Durham Housing Authority and elementary schools, while Chair Wendy Jacobs questioned why county libraries could not host learning centers like Student U and the YMCA.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution against ad-hoc spending from the shrinking COVID reserve without a comprehensive county funding strategy and full public health safeguards.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton supported the centers in principle but criticized making piecemeal funding decisions 'on the fly' without giving staff time to build a strategic plan, and pressed for Exceptional Children priority.
General Manager Joanne Pierce and library leadership cited Urban Libraries Council data and rising youth COVID cases to warn against opening libraries prematurely.
conflicts.resolution: Following partner assurances on DHA/DSS outreach and budget staff confirming COVID reserve capacity, the board approved $405,600 unanimously (5-0).

conflicts.issue: Transportation Demand Management and Charging County Employees for Deck Parking
conflicts.summary: During directives review, commissioners clashed over whether staff should evaluate charging county employees to park in county decks ahead of the 300 and 500 East Main Street parking decisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring forward TDM options including potential employee parking fees to manage parking demand and right-size downtown parking decks.
side_a_arguments: Commissioners Ellen W. Reckhow and Wendy Jacobs noted City of Durham employees pay tiered parking rates and the Environmental Affairs Board urged cutting parking supply in the 300/500 block projects.
conflicts.side_b_position: Protect free employee parking as a matter of workforce fairness and economic equity.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair James Hill argued charging county workers—many single mothers—for parking when Durham transit cannot reliably get parents from schools to downtown work is regressive.
Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton called taking back hard-won competitive employee compensation through parking fees 'inhumane.'
conflicts.resolution: No vote taken; County Manager Wendell Davis agreed to present TDM options and updates at the March work session.

conflicts.issue: Scope, Eligibility, and FEMA Reimbursement Risk of the 10% COVID-19 Hazard Pay Differential
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and county administration clashed over expanding the 10% COVID-19 hazard pay differential to over 1,800 employees (including administrative support and closed-library staff) without formal board policy approval, and over the financial risk if FEMA denies 75% reimbursement or the state declines the remaining 25%.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit hazard pay strictly to clearly frontline/public-facing essential roles, test FEMA eligibility immediately, and preserve lapsed/local dollars for urgent community relief such as eviction prevention.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow noted that the April 29 policy revision added broad 'support services' language and covered 107 library staff despite libraries being closed, risking FEMA disallowance compared to Wake County and the City of Durham (which used CARES Act funds only for frontline/EOC workers).

Chair Jacobs argued that an estimated $1 million local 25% share and reliance on frozen/lapsed salaries constituted major policy choices never brought to the board while 60,000 residents faced potential eviction.

Vice Chair James Hill stated he understood paying deputies, EMTs, and health workers, but questioned hazard pay for staff with no public contact and warned against being stuck with the bill if FEMA denies reimbursement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the existing differential pay structure for both frontline and required on-site administrative support staff as compliant with FEMA rules and necessary for operations and retention.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Wendell Davis, Claudia Hager, and Susan Tezai argued the April 29 document merely clarified a pre-disaster policy, cited cyberattack recovery requiring on-site finance/payroll/AP staff, and emphasized department-head and GM sign-off plus ongoing compliance vetting with FEMA.

Commissioner Heidi Carter expressed deep gratitude for essential staff and asked how confident finance was in compliance (receiving confirmation from Hager) while inquiring about a December sunset plan; Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton emphasized supporting workers on the front lines and asked when FEMA filings would confirm reimbursement.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff committed to filing the initial quarterly FEMA claim promptly, delivering data on total employees, frozen-salary savings, and peer 'Big 10' county policies, and revisiting hazard pay ahead of December.

conflicts.meeting_title: August 10, 2020 BOCC Regular Session Virtual Meeting
conflicts.issue: M/WBE Contracting Commitment on $95,000 'Back on the Bull' Communications Budget Amendment
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton questioned the $264,195 project chart versus the $95,000 consent item and objected that no explicit M/WBE vendor participation requirement appeared in the agenda documentation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require documented M/WBE vendor participation commitments before approving communications funding.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton argued the board committed to M/WBE participation across county contracts and saw no contractual language ensuring African American and minority vendors were hired.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the time-sensitive $95,000 budget amendment for Phases 2 and 3 media buys while directing staff to track and report M/WBE vendor contracting.
side_b_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs and General Manager Jodi Miller noted 57% of planned buys targeted Latinx media and that no vendor contracts were attached yet to the planning budget amendment.
Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow proposed approving the amendment while instructing staff to push for minority vendors and report back on actual contracts.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to convey the board's M/WBE expectation and report back on actual media contracts, and the consent agenda passed 5-0.

conflicts.issue: Joint Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Bylaws and Representation
conflicts.summary: During preliminary review ahead of the July 13 vote, commissioners and Sheriff Clarence Birkhead diverged over whether the City-drafted bylaws fairly involved county leadership, acknowledged existing county criminal justice programs, and included public safety officials.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance the community-led task force promptly in alignment with City Council and School Board expectations, keeping elected officials and department heads off the voting body.
side_a_arguments: Commissioners Heidi Carter and Wendy Jacobs cited strong public demand and noted the task force was modeled like the Pre-K task force to comprise community representatives rather than elected or department leaders.
Chair Jacobs noted Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson welcomed county bylaw revisions and proposed a joint briefing on existing county programs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Revise the bylaws before approval to ensure equal county partnership, reflect existing county criminal justice successes, and give public safety officials a voice.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow objected that the City bypassed the Joint City-County Committee and wrote bylaws focusing on perceived gaps while ignoring Durham's CJRC, Stepping Up initiative, mental health court, and reduced jail population.
Sheriff Clarence Birkhead objected that a public safety task force excluded public safety representation.
conflicts.resolution: Continued to the July 13, 2020 meeting for bylaw revisions and fuller debate.

conflicts.issue: County Manager Wendell Davis's Racial Bias Allegations Against Commissioner Heidi Carter and Scope of Investigation
conflicts.summary: Public speakers, Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton, and Commissioner Heidi Carter clashed over County Manager Wendell Davis's letter accusing Carter of racial bias and demeaning remarks, though all five commissioners ultimately agreed in closed session to seek an independent outside investigation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Validate the County Manager's complaint of racial bias and mistreatment by Commissioner Carter and launch a swift, impartial external investigation.
side_a_arguments: Community speakers (including Joshua Gunn, Omar Beasley, Jackie Wagstaff, and Dr. Lavonia Allison) cited Davis's seven-year exemplary audit record and accused Carter of racial insensitivity and disrespectful remarks ('you work for the board; grin and bear it').
Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton insisted on holding the public comment session before closed session so community voices would be heard.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject allegations of racist intent while agreeing to an independent outside review to address all underlying issues fairly.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter stated she would not apologize for advocating for DPS, pre-K, affordable housing, and transit alongside leaders of color, and joined the vote to enter closed session.
Chair Wendy Jacobs apologized that Davis's feelings were hurt while stating she did not believe Carter intended racist remarks and supporting outside counsel.
conflicts.resolution: After a 30-minute closed session, the board unanimously directed the clerk to contact NCACC for outside counsel recommendations and consult UNC School of Government and ICMA regarding a broad investigation.

conflicts.issue: Neighborhood Character Protection vs. Aggressive Missing-Middle Housing Supply in Expanding Housing Choices
conflicts.summary: During the Expanding Housing Choices briefing, commissioners diverged on how aggressively to loosen urban-tier zoning rules: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow and Vice Chair James Hill emphasized neighborhood fabric, Neighborhood Protection Overlays (NPOs), and gentrification/absentee-investor risks, while Commissioner Heidi Carter urged prioritizing maximum housing supply and future affordability over existing neighborhood preservation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize protecting existing neighborhood fabric, honoring Neighborhood Protection Overlays, and guarding against speculative investor conversions and displacement in lower-income neighborhoods.
side_a_arguments: Overriding NPO provisions undermines extensive community work put into overlays like Old West Durham and Tuscaloosa-Lakewood.
Dividing a block face into six small lots in a row would create a tear in the fabric of established neighborhoods; clustered cottage courts or zero-lot-line designs would be more context-sensitive.
Without owner-occupancy rules, outside investors in less affluent neighborhoods could buy properties solely to maximize units without caring about neighborhood character, compounding gentrification.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pursue missing-middle housing supply and urban-tier density as aggressively as possible to address Durham's affordability crisis for future and current residents.
side_b_arguments: Expanding housing options and missing-middle supply should be the board's primary driver rather than preserving existing neighborhood fabric through overlays.
With 160,000 new residents projected over 25–30 years, failing to expand in-town supply will drive worse unaffordability, sprawl, and climate/infrastructure costs.
Suburban neighborhoods should also be examined for duplex and townhome opportunities where covenants do not prohibit them.
conflicts.resolution: Informational work-session discussion with no formal vote; Planning Director Patrick Young committed to refining context-sensitive standards with neighborhood groups ahead of the February 12, 2019 Planning Commission public hearing and April/May 2019 board vote.

conflicts.issue: Automatic County Manager Sign-Off Authority for Future IT Contract Renewals (Item 561)
conflicts.summary: During work session review of the $82,199.44 NetApp storage support renewal, commissioners challenged proposed agenda language granting the County Manager automatic sign-off on future annual renewals and amendments without board approval.
conflicts.side_a_position: Preserve annual Board of County Commissioners oversight over multi-year contract renewals and potential price increases rather than delegating automatic sign-off.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs noted that annual renewals cross into future approved budgets and could involve cost changes that normally require board approval.
Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioned whether a contract rising by $75,000 within an IT operational fund would bypass board review under the proposed wording.
conflicts.side_b_position: Allow administrative renewal sign-off for time-sensitive IT maintenance agreements already budgeted within existing departmental operational funds.
side_b_arguments: IS&T staff (Antonio Davis) and Budget staff (David Ades) explained that maintenance renewals are anticipated in each year's operational budget and kept within appropriated departmental funds.
conflicts.resolution: Finance/Purchasing staff (Claudia) recommended removing the automatic sign-off language and proceeding via the traditional board-approval route.

conflicts.issue: M/WBE Participation and Local Hiring Accountability in the UNC Back on the Bull Community Health Ambassadors ILA (Item 539)
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton challenged the interlocal agreement transferring county funds to the City of Durham for UNC Gillings School of Public Health's Community Health Ambassadors contract, arguing it lacked explicit M/WBE participation and local Durham hiring protections.
conflicts.side_a_position: Contracts funded with county tax dollars should explicitly document M/WBE participation and local Durham equity hiring standards rather than deferring to an outside university's procurement rules.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton noted the agenda materials contained no M/WBE provisions and questioned why Chapel Hill-based UNC would control hiring for a Durham community program without documented local diversity and equity commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: The ILA transfers previously approved funds to the City for a scope already geared toward hiring diverse Durham residents to assist businesses of color, and staff can follow up on UNC/City hiring practices.
side_b_arguments: General Manager Jodi Miller explained the ILA simply transfers funds approved on August 24 to the City to contract with UNC, and committed to obtaining UNC and City recruitment/hiring strategies via email.
Chair Wendy Jacobs pointed out that the attached scope of work specified at least 4 of 10 ambassadors must be Latinx and that the program serves businesses and communities of color.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to follow up with the City and UNC to provide written recruitment and equity-hiring details ahead of final consent approval.

conflicts.issue: Board Oversight of COVID-19 Hazard Pay Differential and Use of Lapsed Salaries
conflicts.summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow criticized the administration's $3 million hazard pay expenditure and reliance on frozen/lapsed salaries without explicit board policy approval.
conflicts.side_a_position: Multi-million-dollar hazard pay decisions and the repurposing of frozen-position lapsed salaries have major budget trade-offs and require direct board policy review and clear eligibility boundaries.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs noted the City of Durham ended hazard pay on June 19 at $433,000, questioned reports of staff opting to work on-site qualifying for differential pay, and stated she had assumed salary freezes would preserve funds for broader community needs.
Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioned how long hazard pay would continue and urged clear boundaries and follow-up documentation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hazard pay was a necessary workforce retention and emergency response measure largely offset by CARES Act and projected 75%/25% FEMA/state reimbursements.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Wendell Davis and Claudia Hager argued the 10% differential prevented retirements/turnover, projected a net local cost of roughly $791,000, and noted peer counties were evaluating hazard pay through December.
conflicts.resolution: Board scheduled a dedicated public discussion of FEMA guidelines and hazard pay policy for the upcoming October 13 regular meeting.

conflicts.issue: Nonprofit RFP Redesign: Inclusion of Housing Security and Review Timeline (Item 20-0487)
conflicts.summary: Commissioners debated whether the redesigned nonprofit RFP should include housing security alongside food security, youth enrichment, and workforce development, and pressed staff on oversight expertise and tight fall deadlines.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit the redesigned pilot RFP to three areas where the county has dedicated subject-matter expertise rather than splitting limited funds four ways.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioned whether housing fell inside the county's core expertise and staffing capacity, suggesting three focused areas might produce stronger results with $353,750 in bridge funding.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain housing security as one of the four priority target areas and coordinate oversight with DSS and existing community partnerships.
side_b_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs noted housing repairs, financial literacy, and land conservancy needs made housing a top community priority, and Deputy Manager Claudia Hager argued DSS housing partnerships could cover oversight.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioner Reckhow accepted keeping all four target areas, and the board gave consensus direction to launch the RFP while tightening the award timeline and keeping commissioners informed.

conflicts.issue: County Facility Use (Libraries) and Funding Urgency for HOPE Learning Centers
conflicts.summary: During the DPS virtual learning and budget updates, commissioners and school leaders confronted tension over whether the County could immediately open empty library facilities and commit scarce local/CARES funds for HOPE Learning Centers before September 8.
conflicts.side_a_position: Urgently assess County libraries, volunteer staff, and Round 2 CARES funds to provide free learning-center seats and digital equity for the most vulnerable students.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow noted the new Main Library sat empty with technology resources and directed the County Manager to return by August 24 with a facilities, staffing, and funding assessment.
BOE members (including Jovonia Lewis) stressed that 83% of DPS students are Black and brown and urged prioritizing free learning-center seats despite Community Ed shortfalls.
conflicts.side_b_position: County administration cautioned that it had not been included in initial cost projections and faced declining revenues and limited fund balance.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Wendell Davis stated County staff had not been directly involved in the HOPE Center cost numbers, noted revenue slowdowns and limited discretionary pots beyond fund balance, and committed to analyzing the $3.3 million county share of Round 2 CARES funding.
conflicts.resolution: Board directed County staff to complete a facilities, staffing, and CARES/fund-balance analysis ahead of the August 24 BOCC regular session.

conflicts.issue: Raising Confederate Monument Base Removal During Racism Resolution Discussion
conflicts.summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs read letters calling for removal of the remaining Confederate monument base as a public health hazard, while Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton objected to bringing it up when the County Attorney advised waiting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Connect the Racism as a Public Health Crisis resolution to declaring the Confederate monument base a public health and safety hazard for removal.
side_a_arguments: Confederate Monuments Commission co-chairs and Mayor Steve Schewel wrote urging BOCC to act because white supremacist symbols inflict measurable stress and harm on Black residents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not force the monument onto the evening's agenda against the County Attorney's advice when the urgent focus is preventing Black and brown people from being killed.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Howerton noted the board had already agreed to hold the monument off the agenda for staff legal research and urged keeping focus on immediate threats to life.
conflicts.resolution: Chair Jacobs clarified no action on the monument was on the June 8/9 agenda and moved to the next agenda item.

conflicts.issue: Budget Amendment Motion: Full $3.8 Million Funding for DPS Classified Staff $15/Hour Minimum Wage
conflicts.summary: Motion to pull $3.8M from fund balance/COVID reserves to lift all DPS classified staff to $15/hour in FY 2020–21 failed 2-3, leaving the ~$1.9M half-step increase in place for potential January 2021 mid-year review.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-3)

conflicts.issue: TC190001 Sedimentation/Erosion Control Regulations and Fill-Site Enforcement
conflicts.summary: Following resident testimony detailing non-compliant fill sites, concrete debris on Betty Ross Road, and DOT diamond-grinding dumping near Falls Lake, commissioners debated whether to adopt the City-approved Omnibus Changes 13 text amendment immediately alongside a task force review or hold/modify provisions such as the 30-foot stockpile rule and compliance enforcement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the pending TC190001 regulations now (matching the City) while commissioning a task force with the Soil and Water Conservation Board, Environmental Affairs Board, and NC State to bring back enforcement and legislative amendments.
side_a_arguments: The City of Durham had already approved the omnibus ordinance.
Staff committed to convening a task force for monitoring, enforcement, and near-term amendments in the new year.
conflicts.side_b_position: One present commissioner (either Wendy Jacobs or James Hill, not named in the audio transcript) voted against the initial combined approval motion at 02:21:58 amid concerns raised about the 30-foot stockpile provision and unresolved compliance enforcement.
side_b_arguments: Residents warned that current fill-site enforcement and the 30-foot stockpile language failed to protect Falls Lake watershed residents.
conflicts.resolution: The preliminary combined motion passed 3-1 (with Ellen W. Reckhow and Heidi Carter moving/seconding in favor, and one unidentified present member between Wendy Jacobs and James Hill opposed); when prompted for formal statutory votes, the board unanimously approved both the consistency statement (4-0) and the ordinance with the task force directive (4-0).

conflicts.issue: Setting the County Manager's Salary at $226,011
conflicts.summary: Following a pre-meeting closed session, the board split 4-1 on setting the County Manager's salary at $226,011.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve setting the County Manager's salary at $226,011.
side_a_arguments: Supported by four commissioners following closed-session personnel review.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose setting the County Manager's salary at $226,011.
side_b_arguments: One commissioner voted nay without stating remarks on the open-session record.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-1 on a motion by Ellen W. Reckhow and second by James Hill; the audio transcript truncated the dissenting commissioner's name among Wendy Jacobs, Brenda A. Howerton, and Heidi Carter.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham County BOCC Work Session Dec 3 LIve
conflicts.issue: 2019 Board Meeting Calendar and Second Monthly Work Session Proposal
conflicts.summary: During review of the proposed 2019 meeting schedule, Commissioner Heidi Carter declined to approve dates past June and advocated adding a second work session on Thursday afternoons, whereas Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton urged approving at least through August for planning purposes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 2019 schedule only through June 2019 and revisit adding a second monthly work session on Thursday afternoons following Monday regular meetings.
side_a_arguments: Adding a second work session respects staff time and gives the board adequate advance review.
Moving work sessions to Thursday afternoons following Monday night regular meetings improves workflow before locking in the second half of the year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the meeting schedule at least through August 2019 so commissioners have certainty for advance planning.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners need confirmed dates through at least August to organize personal and professional calendars without shifting meeting dates.
conflicts.resolution: No vote was taken; Chair Wendy Jacobs and staff agreed to return at a January meeting with revised calendar options and printed schedule comparisons.

conflicts.issue: County Attorney Salary Adjustment ($204,811)
conflicts.summary: After adjourning from closed session, the board split 4-1 by voice vote on setting the County Attorney's salary at $204,811 effective on his anniversary date.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve setting the County Attorney's salary at $204,811 effective on the anniversary date.
side_a_arguments: Ellen W. Reckhow moved and Heidi Carter seconded the post-closed-session salary adjustment without extended open-session floor debate.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the proposed $204,811 salary adjustment.
side_b_arguments: One commissioner voted Nay during the voice vote without stating reasons on the open-session record.
conflicts.resolution: Motion carried 4-1; the individual dissenting commissioner and the other two Aye voters were not identified by name in the audio transcript.

conflicts.issue: Adoption of FY 2020–2021 County Budget Ordinance (as Amended with Cooperative Extension Position)
conflicts.summary: Adopted FY21 budget ordinance incorporating ~$5M+ in new DPS funding (including $1.9M toward $15/hr classified wages), a full-time Spanish interpreter, broadband study, $1M small business fund, food security coordinator, and the $42,714 Cooperative Extension amendment. Carter and Jacobs voted No solely because full $15/hr DPS classified funding was omitted.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 3-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (3-2)

meetings.title: Durham County Government BOCC Live Nov 23, 2020
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs presided over the November 23, 2020 regular session—the final meeting of the 2016–2020 board—which featured farewell tributes and plaques honoring outgoing Vice Chair James Hill (4 years) and outgoing Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow (32 years, tying Durham County's longevity record). The board unanimously approved four sets of prior meeting minutes (5-0), celebrated the 2020 ETI Solutions sustainability award for energy retrofits, and voted 5-0 to extend the meeting to 11:30 p.m. On pandemic fiscal items, the board unanimously approved a budget amendment and revised CARES Act funding plan (5-0) redirecting funds toward small business needs before the federal deadline, unanimously directed the County Manager to study how Wake and Mecklenburg counties were scaling back employee hazard pay with cost projections (5-0), and unanimously directed staff to work with Durham Public Schools on a financial plan for a $15/hour minimum wage for DPS classified employees ahead of January budget reviews (5-0).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, and Community Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the meeting with the public charge and a moment of silence honoring outgoing Commissioners Ellen W. Reckhow and James Hill. Chair Jacobs shared announcements on ACA Marketplace enrollment (December 15 deadline), North Carolina's $335 Extra Credit Grant (extended to December 7), Durham Tech's Back to Work Initiative, free COVID-19 testing through December 3, and Thanksgiving safety guidance.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Prior Meeting Minutes (Oct. 12, Oct. 26, Nov. 2, and Nov. 9, 2020)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board commended clerk staff for catching up on four sets of minutes (October 12 regular, October 26 regular, November 2 work session, and November 9 regular sessions) and approved them 5-0 by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognition: 2020 ETI Solutions Sustainability Award
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sustainability Manager Tobin Freid, Deputy Director Perry Mange, and software partner Mr. Kaufman presented Durham County's receipt of the 2020 ETI Solutions Award for using empirical energy data to track greenhouse gas reductions, highlighting a Hillsborough warehouse LED retrofit achieving over 40% energy savings and >100% ROI.

agenda_items.title: Tributes and Service Plaques for Outgoing Commissioners James Hill and Ellen W. Reckhow
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners presented appreciation plaques and farewell remarks honoring Vice Chair James Hill for four years of service and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow for 32 years of service (1988–2020), tying G.H. Kirkland's county record for longevity.

agenda_items.title: CARES Act Revised Funding Plan, Budget Amendment, and Meeting Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reviewed shifting $250,000 originally contemplated for small-business PPE toward direct small business grants via electronic funds transfer alongside $44,200 in related adjustments ahead of the December 30 federal deadline. After voting 5-0 to extend the meeting until 11:30 p.m., the board voted 5-0 on Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow's motion to approve the budget amendment and revised CARES Act funding plan.

agenda_items.title: County Employee Hazard Pay Scale-Back Study Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Expressing concern over ongoing unbudgeted COVID expenses without a new federal relief package, Commissioner Reckhow moved to pause/examine hazard pay by directing the County Manager to review Wake and Mecklenburg counties' plans and return with an approach for scaling back, including cost projections and funding sources. The motion passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Financial Plan for $15/Hour Minimum Salary for DPS Classified Employees
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter moved to ask the County Manager and staff to collaborate with Durham Public Schools to develop a cost estimate and financial plan to implement a $15/hour salary for all DPS classified employees, to be considered in January alongside property/sales tax updates and the county audit. Seconded by Commissioner Reckhow as consistent with the board's June commitment, the motion passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following brief board and commission appointment business (including the Community Wellness Task Force), the board voted 5-0 to enter closed session at 04:15:11 and returned at 04:31:51 for Commissioner Reckhow's final motion to adjourn.

votes.item_title: Approval of Meeting Minutes (Oct. 12, Oct. 26, Nov. 2, and Nov. 9, 2020)
votes.discussion_detail: Approved four backlogged sets of minutes prepared by the clerk's office.

votes.item_title: Motion to Extend Meeting Time Until 11:30 PM
votes.discussion_detail: Extended the meeting to 11:30 p.m. to finish CARES Act, hazard pay, and DPS compensation items.

votes.item_title: Approval of Budget Amendment and Revised CARES Act Funding Plan
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the budget amendment and revised CARES Act plan ahead of the December 30 spending deadline, followed by discussion of reallocating $250,000 for small business grants and $44,200 in related expenditures.

votes.item_title: Direct County Manager to Review Wake and Mecklenburg Hazard Pay Plans and Return with Scale-Back Approach
votes.discussion_detail: Requested the County Manager to benchmark Wake and Mecklenburg counties' hazard pay policies and bring back a scale-back plan with cost projections and funding sources.

votes.item_title: Direct Staff to Develop Cost Estimate and Financial Plan for $15/Hour Minimum Salary for DPS Classified Employees
votes.notes: All commissioners expressed support; vote declared unanimous at 04:08:59.
votes.discussion_detail: Directed county staff to work with DPS on a cost estimate and funding plan for implementing $15/hour pay for DPS classified employees for January consideration alongside tax revenue and audit updates.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session
votes.discussion_detail: Entered closed session briefly before returning to adjourn at 04:31:51.

meetings.title: Durham County Government BOCC Live November 9, 2020
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs presided over the November 9, 2020 regular session, opening with reflections on the historic November 2020 election—nearly 73% voter turnout in Durham, Vice President-elect Kamala Harris, and incoming commissioners Nimasheena Burns and Nida Allam. The board unanimously approved the September 28 and October 5 minutes (5-0), presented a 2020 Veterans Day resolution honoring roughly 15,000 county veterans, and approved the consent agenda (5-0) including the Back on the Bull campaign, McFarland farmland easement, and renewable energy plan funding. In a substantive fiscal discussion, commissioners and finance staff examined $1.4 million in unbudgeted FY2021 hazard pay (projecting $5–6 million annualized), CARES Act reimbursement limits ahead of December 30, protecting the county's AAA bond rating, and an earlier June vote declining a $15/hour floor before entering closed session (5-0) under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Reflections on the 2020 Election
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m., read the public charge, and joined Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton in reflecting on the historic 2020 election, including Kamala Harris's election as Vice President, ~73% Durham voter turnout, and incoming commissioners Nimasheena Burns and Nida Allam.

agenda_items.title: Approval of September 28 and October 5, 2020 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow moved and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton seconded approval of the September 28, 2020 regular session and October 5, 2020 work session minutes, which passed 5-0 by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Resolution for Veterans Day 2020
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Jacobs read the Durham BOCC Resolution for Veterans Day 2020 honoring nearly 15,000 Durham County veterans. Veterans Services Director Lois Harvin-Ravin and staff coordinators Jonathan and Lindsay Atkins outlined the November 11 virtual ceremony and drive-thru recognition event.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Moved by Commissioner Reckhow and seconded by Commissioner Carter, the consent agenda was approved; Chair Jacobs highlighted continued funding for the Back on the Bull public health media campaign, the McFarland farmland protection easement, and funding for the county's renewable energy plan.

agenda_items.title: CARES Act Reimbursement, Hazard Pay Fiscal Impact, and Fund Balance Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners and finance staff (Susan and Manager Davis) reviewed $1.4 million spent to date in FY2021 on unbudgeted hazard pay—projecting $5–6 million annualized—and benchmarked six peer counties (five of which ended hazard pay after 2–3 months). Staff noted the current CARES Act plan capped salaries and benefits at $1.8 million pending a revised final plan before December 30, discussed potential small business grant uses and protecting the AAA bond rating, and heard Commissioners Howerton and Hill reflect on staff pandemic sacrifices and the June $15/hour wage vote.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session on Personnel / Investigation Matter (N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 5-0 to enter closed session to consider personnel qualifications, performance, or complaints/grievances involving an individual public officer or employee under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6).

votes.item_title: Approval of September 28 and October 5, 2020 Meeting Minutes
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the September 28, 2020 regular session and October 5, 2020 work session minutes.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session (N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6))
votes.discussion_detail: Entered closed session to consider personnel performance/complaint matters.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session - November 2, 2020
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 2, 2020 work session held on Election Eve, Chair Wendy Jacobs and the board reviewed consent agenda items, environmental ordinance revisions, county facility siting, and health partnerships without taking formal votes other than adjournment. During consent review of Item 561 (an $82,199.44 NetApp storage support renewal), Chair Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow challenged contract language that would allow the County Manager to sign off automatically on subsequent annual renewals without returning to the Board, prompting Finance and Purchasing staff to recommend removing the clause and keeping traditional board review. Staff also presented proposed stormwater and erosion control ordinance changes bringing stream determinations in-house, a Junction Road update proposing to co-locate the Animal Shelter and Public Safety Service Center on 60 county-owned industrial acres, and a letter of support request for Alliance Health's Medicaid Tailored Plan application.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comments Check
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the Election Eve work session and confirmed with the clerk's office that no citizen comments had been submitted by the Sunday noon deadline.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review: Item 561 (NetApp Automatic Renewal Authority) and Transit/Parking
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The County Manager introduced Item 561 ($82,199.44 FY2021 NetApp storage support renewal), and Chair Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioned language authorizing the County Manager to automatically sign off on future annual maintenance renewals and amendments without returning to the board. After IS&T, Budget (David Ades), and Finance/Purchasing (Claudia) explained operational budget flexibility versus board oversight, Purchasing recommended removing the automatic sign-off language; commissioners also highlighted 15-minute bus connectivity to Health and Human Services and remote-work carbon reductions.

agenda_items.title: Stormwater and Erosion Control Ordinance Revisions (Stream Determinations and Permitting)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Environmental staff (Mackenzie and Ryan) and Senior Assistant County Attorney Larissa Williamson presented draft stormwater ordinance updates bringing stream determination field evaluations in-house and revising site-plan, construction-drawing, and as-built permitting workflows to better protect water quality and neighboring properties. Board members expressed support for bringing the revised ordinance to public hearing and adoption at the next meeting.

agenda_items.title: Junction Road Site Update (Proposed Animal Shelter and Public Safety Center Siting)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jay Gibson and Perry Mange reviewed the Junction Road property history—noting the 2017 withdrawal of heavy industrial rezoning on 40 acres after community opposition, leaving 60 industrial-zoned acres—and outlined plans to potentially co-locate a new Animal Shelter (four minutes from the existing shelter) and Public Safety Service Center / EOC facilities. Staff indicated a comprehensive package and EOC feasibility results would return around February.

agenda_items.title: Alliance Health Tailored Plan Letter of Support and Manager Directives Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Rob Robinson briefed the board on Medicaid transformation and Alliance Health's Tailored Plan application for behavioral health management, and staff provided updates on legislative tracking and the My Brother's Keeper (MBK) advisory committee before the board adjourned.

disagreements.issue: Automatic County Manager Sign-Off Authority for Future IT Contract Renewals (Item 561)
disagreements.summary: During work session review of the $82,199.44 NetApp storage support renewal, commissioners challenged proposed agenda language granting the County Manager automatic sign-off on future annual renewals and amendments without board approval.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve annual Board of County Commissioners oversight over multi-year contract renewals and potential price increases rather than delegating automatic sign-off.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs noted that annual renewals cross into future approved budgets and could involve cost changes that normally require board approval.
Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioned whether a contract rising by $75,000 within an IT operational fund would bypass board review under the proposed wording.
disagreements.side_b_position: Allow administrative renewal sign-off for time-sensitive IT maintenance agreements already budgeted within existing departmental operational funds.
side_b_arguments: IS&T staff (Antonio Davis) and Budget staff (David Ades) explained that maintenance renewals are anticipated in each year's operational budget and kept within appropriated departmental funds.
disagreements.resolution: Finance/Purchasing staff (Claudia) recommended removing the automatic sign-off language and proceeding via the traditional board-approval route.

meetings.title: Durham County Government BOCC Live
meetings.executive_summary: At the October 27, 2020 meeting presided over by Chair Wendy Jacobs, the Durham Racial Equity Task Force presented its report, 'An Urgent and Loving Call to Action,' covering health and environment, education, and public history recommendations. Subcommittee leaders urged compensating marginalized residents on advisory boards, creating a City-County Health Alliance, increasing COVID-19 transparency in the county jail, funding universal Pre-K, and shifting county funds from 27 budgeted School Resource Officers to full-time school nurses, counselors, and social workers. The board also received a COVID-19 public health update reporting 8,922 cumulative cases and Duke Health food/relief assistance, received ballot tabulations appointing two advisory board members, and voted 5-0 to enter closed session for attorney-client consultation before returning to adjourn.

agenda_items.title: Racial Equity Task Force Report: 'An Urgent and Loving Call to Action'
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Subcommittee leaders presented the Racial Equity Task Force's recommendations, led by Jamal Moss (Health & Environment) calling for community-rooted engagement, compensating marginalized residents on boards, a City-County Health Alliance, annual equity/trauma training for first responders, jail COVID-19 transparency, and community land-use control. The Education Subcommittee urged funding universal Pre-K and reallocating funds from 27 budgeted School Resource Officers to full-time school nurses, counselors, and social workers to prevent the school-to-prison pipeline, while Public History advocated inclusive county storytelling and public art.

agenda_items.title: Board and Chief Racial Equity Officer Discussion of Task Force Implementation and Data
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners and the county's Chief Racial Equity Officer discussed aligning the six task force focus areas with county priorities, paying community members as qualitative data consultants, partnering with DataWorks and local universities, and exploring tax assistance grants. agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments

agenda_items.title: Community Announcements: Early Voting, COVID-19 Relief Programs, and Transit Feedback

meetings.title: Durham County Government BOCC Live
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs presided over the October 13, 2020 meeting with all five seated commissioners participating virtually. The board unanimously approved the August 24, 2020 minutes (5-0), adopted proclamations recognizing Domestic Workers Day and National Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and approved the consent agenda (5-0) after questioning funding sources for a screener contract amendment (20-0468) and recognizing Watts Street Baptist Church's donation to Bull City United. Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 403 active COVID-19 cases, 98 total deaths, and persistent racial disparities alongside Duke Population Health wraparound support services. Commissioners then engaged in an extended policy debate—without taking a formal vote—over the county's 10% COVID-19 hazard pay differential, with Chair Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow questioning the April 29 expansion to support staff (including closed-library workers) and reliance on lapsed salaries and uncertain FEMA reimbursements while County Manager Wendell Davis and finance staff defended the policy as FEMA-compliant and vital to operations before the board adjourned unanimously (5-0) to closed session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Approval of August 24, 2020 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Wendy Jacobs delivered the public charge, held a moment of reflection, and presented announcements covering COVID nonprofit grant info sessions, the October 31 census deadline, early voting, Project Access medical equipment loans, the Durham County Transit Plan survey, and Halloween safety guidance. Commissioners then unanimously approved the August 24, 2020 meeting minutes by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations: Domestic Workers Day and National Cybersecurity Awareness Month
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Jacobs read a proclamation recognizing Domestic Workers Day (October 12, 2020), with National Domestic Workers Alliance and We Dream in Black representatives thanking the board and highlighting PPE shortages and living-wage needs. At 01:02:19, Commissioner Heidi Carter read a proclamation designating October 2020 as National Cybersecurity Awareness Month, praising IT staff for cyberattack recovery and remote-work continuity.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Screener Contract 20-0468 and Bull City United Donation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners reviewed the consent agenda, focusing on Item 20-0468 increasing the building screener contract, and questioned why the agenda form omitted the funding source. Staff explained the cost would be covered through lapsed salaries within the operating budget, and Chair Jacobs later noted that the Bull City United donation on the agenda came from Watts Street Baptist Church before the board unanimously approved the consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: Public Health COVID-19 Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported a slight uptick to 403 active cases, 98 cumulative deaths, and 8,320 total cases, with Hispanic/Latinx residents representing 46.78% and Black residents 30.41% of recent cases. He detailed wraparound isolation support delivered through Duke Population Health (food, $400 relief payments, and rent assistance) and credited the 10% hazard pay differential with helping retain public health workers.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of FEMA Guidelines, COVID-19 Hazard Pay Differential, and Lapsed Salaries
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners debated the scope and fiscal risk of the county's 10% hazard pay differential, which expanded from 1,700+ employees in spring to over 1,800 since July 1 and projected roughly $3 million in combined hazard pay and overtime for FEMA reimbursement. Chair Jacobs and Commissioner Reckhow questioned covering non-public-facing support staff and 107 library workers while libraries were closed, as well as using frozen/lapsed salaries without explicit board policy approval, while County Manager Wendell Davis, Claudia Hager, and Susan Tezai defended the policy's compliance with FEMA guidelines and promised follow-up data on frozen positions and peer county practices.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session on Economic Development Incentives (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the hazard pay discussion, the board voted unanimously to adjourn into closed session to discuss industrial location or expansion and tentative economic development incentives before reconvening at 11:00 p.m. to adjourn.

votes.item_title: Approval of August 24, 2020 BOCC Meeting Minutes
votes.notes: Chair Jacobs announced the minutes were unanimously approved after polling Hill, Howerton, Carter, and Reckhow.
votes.discussion_detail: No corrections were requested prior to the voice vote approving the August 24, 2020 minutes.

votes.item_title: Motion to Adjourn to Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4))
votes.discussion_detail: Board moved into closed session to discuss location/expansion of businesses and tentative economic development incentives.

disagreements.issue: Scope, Eligibility, and FEMA Reimbursement Risk of the 10% COVID-19 Hazard Pay Differential
disagreements.summary: Commissioners and county administration clashed over expanding the 10% COVID-19 hazard pay differential to over 1,800 employees (including administrative support and closed-library staff) without formal board policy approval, and over the financial risk if FEMA denies 75% reimbursement or the state declines the remaining 25%.
disagreements.side_a_position: Limit hazard pay strictly to clearly frontline/public-facing essential roles, test FEMA eligibility immediately, and preserve lapsed/local dollars for urgent community relief such as eviction prevention.
side_a_arguments: Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Ellen W. Reckhow noted that the April 29 policy revision added broad 'support services' language and covered 107 library staff despite libraries being closed, risking FEMA disallowance compared to Wake County and the City of Durham (which used CARES Act funds only for frontline/EOC workers).

Chair Jacobs argued that an estimated $1 million local 25% share and reliance on frozen/lapsed salaries constituted major policy choices never brought to the board while 60,000 residents faced potential eviction.

Vice Chair James Hill stated he understood paying deputies, EMTs, and health workers, but questioned hazard pay for staff with no public contact and warned against being stuck with the bill if FEMA denies reimbursement.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain the existing differential pay structure for both frontline and required on-site administrative support staff as compliant with FEMA rules and necessary for operations and retention.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Wendell Davis, Claudia Hager, and Susan Tezai argued the April 29 document merely clarified a pre-disaster policy, cited cyberattack recovery requiring on-site finance/payroll/AP staff, and emphasized department-head and GM sign-off plus ongoing compliance vetting with FEMA.

Commissioner Heidi Carter expressed deep gratitude for essential staff and asked how confident finance was in compliance (receiving confirmation from Hager) while inquiring about a December sunset plan; Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton emphasized supporting workers on the front lines and asked when FEMA filings would confirm reimbursement.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff committed to filing the initial quarterly FEMA claim promptly, delivering data on total employees, frozen-salary savings, and peer 'Big 10' county policies, and revisiting hazard pay ahead of December.
